result: PGE2 inhibits Kv2.2 currents in HEK293T cells in a dose-dependent manner, with maximal effect at 10 μM, reaching maximum inhibition in approximately 6 minutes. The inhibition occurs at all positive testing potentials above +20 mV without altering steady-state activation and inactivation properties.
evaluation: Claims C36-C40 are supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A-F. The dose-response relationship, time course, voltage-dependence, and lack of effect on channel gating properties are all demonstrated with appropriate electrophysiological recordings and statistical analyses.

result: PGE2 inhibits Kv2.2 channels via EP2 and EP4 receptors. All four EP receptors (EP1-4) are expressed in HEK293T cells, but only EP2 and EP4 antagonists block PGE2-induced inhibition, and EP2/EP4 agonists mimic PGE2 effects.
evaluation: Claims C41-C48 are supported by mRNA expression data (Figure 2A), immunofluorescence (Figure 2B), and pharmacological experiments with selective antagonists and agonists (Figure 2C-G). The convergent evidence from multiple approaches strongly supports EP2/EP4 mediation.

result: PGE2 inhibits Kv2.2 currents through the PKA signaling pathway. PGE2 rapidly increases PKA activity, PKA activator mimics PGE2 effects, and PKA inhibitor blocks PGE2-induced inhibition.
evaluation: Claims C49-C53 are supported by Western blot showing PKA phosphorylation (Figure 3A) and electrophysiological experiments with PKA activator and inhibitor (Figure 3B-D). The pharmacological evidence clearly demonstrates PKA involvement in the signaling pathway.

result: The S448 residue of Kv2.2 is responsible for PKA-dependent modulation. Among nine putative PKA phosphorylation sites, only S448D mutation significantly reduced Kv2.2 currents and abrogated PGE2 effects, as did the S448A mutation.
evaluation: Claims C54-C58 are supported by computational prediction (Scansite database) and mutagenesis experiments (Figure 3E-H). The convergent evidence from phosphomimetic (S448D) and non-phosphorylatable (S448A) mutations strongly supports S448 as the critical phosphorylation site.

result: PGE2 inhibits endogenous Kv2.2 currents in INS-1(832/13) β-cells. Kv2.2 channels are expressed in these cells, PGE2 inhibits voltage-dependent K+ currents, and knockdown of Kcnb2 reduces currents and abrogates PGE2 effects.
evaluation: Claims C60-C63 are supported by immunofluorescence (Figure 4A), electrophysiological recordings (Figure 4B), and shRNA knockdown experiments (Figure 4C-F). The loss-of-function approach provides strong evidence for Kv2.2 involvement in native β-cells.

result: EP2 and EP4 receptors mediate PGE2 inhibition of K+ currents in INS-1(832/13) cells. EP2 and EP4 agonists inhibit K+ currents, and EP2/EP4 antagonists partially block PGE2-induced inhibition.
evaluation: Claims C64-C66 are supported by pharmacological experiments with selective agonists (Figure 4G-H) and antagonists (Figure 4I-J). The results parallel those in HEK293T cells, confirming the same signaling pathway operates in β-cells.

result: PGE2 reduces electrical activity in INS-1(832/13) cells via Kv2.2 channels. PGE2 reduces action potential frequency and increases half-width without affecting peak amplitude, and Kcnb2 knockdown abrogates these effects.
evaluation: Claims C67-C71 are supported by current-clamp recordings (Figure 5A-C). The loss-of-function approach with shRNA knockdown provides strong evidence that Kv2.2 mediates PGE2 effects on β-cell electrical activity.

result: All four EP receptors (EP1-4) are expressed in INS-1(832/13) cells and in both mouse and human islet β-cells.
evaluation: Claims C72-C73 are supported by immunofluorescence data (Figure 5D-E). The antibody specificity was validated using siRNA knockdown (Figure 5—figure supplement 1), strengthening confidence in the expression data.

result: EP2 and EP4 receptor agonists inhibit action potential frequency in INS-1(832/13) cells, indicating that PGE2 reduces electrical activity via EP2/4 receptors.
evaluation: Claims C74-C76 are supported by current-clamp recordings with selective agonists (Figure 6A-B). The pharmacological evidence confirms that EP2/EP4 receptors mediate PGE2 effects on β-cell electrical activity.

result: PGE2 regulates insulin secretion through Kv2.2 channels in INS-1(832/13) cells. PGE2 reduces GSIS without affecting basal secretion, Kcnb2 knockdown reduces GSIS and alleviates PGE2 inhibition, and overexpression of S448A mutant attenuates PGE2 effects.
evaluation: Claims C77-C80 are supported by insulin secretion assays (Figure 7A-C). The convergent evidence from knockdown and phosphorylation-deficient mutant overexpression strongly supports the role of Kv2.2 and S448 phosphorylation in GSIS regulation.

result: PGE2 modulates glucose tolerance in vivo through Kv2.2 channels. Kcnb2−/− mice have normal fasting glucose, PGE2 worsens glucose tolerance in control but not knockout mice, suggesting Kv2.2 mediates PGE2 effects in vivo.
evaluation: Claims C81-C83 are supported by glucose tolerance tests in Kcnb2 knockout mice (Figure 7D). The loss of PGE2 effect in knockout animals provides strong in vivo evidence for Kv2.2 involvement, though the global knockout limits cell-type specificity.

result: Islets from Kcnb2−/− mice exhibit reduced GSIS compared to wild-type, and PGE2 reduces GSIS in wild-type but not knockout islets.
evaluation: Claims C84-C86 are supported by ex vivo insulin secretion assays from isolated islets (Figure 7E). The data confirm that Kv2.2 is required for both normal GSIS and PGE2-mediated inhibition at the islet level.

result: Kv2.2 ablation reduces K+ current amplitude in mouse β-cells and abolishes PGE2-induced inhibition of K+ currents.
evaluation: Claims C87-C89 are supported by electrophysiological recordings from β-cells within islets (Figure 8A-B). The data confirm that Kv2.2 contributes to native K+ currents and mediates PGE2 effects in primary mouse β-cells.

result: PGE2 reduces action potential firing frequency in β-cells within islets without affecting peak amplitude or half-width, and Kcnb2 knockout abrogates this effect.
evaluation: Claims C90-C92 are supported by current-clamp recordings from β-cells in intact islets (Figure 8C-D). The data confirm that Kv2.2 mediates PGE2 effects on electrical activity in the native islet environment.

result: This study demonstrates that Kv2.2 channels play a crucial role in regulating β-cell repetitive firing and insulin secretion, and that PGE2 inhibits Kv2.2 via the EP2/4-PKA signaling pathway to impede GSIS in normal β-cells.
evaluation: Claims C94, C95, and C114 represent the main conclusions of the study, which are well-supported by the comprehensive experimental evidence from multiple complementary approaches including heterologous expression, cell lines, isolated islets, and knockout mice.

result: PGE2 is the major prostaglandin in pancreatic islets, acts as an endogenous inhibitor of GSIS, plays an important role in T2DM, and has been demonstrated to inhibit GSIS in diabetic models. Plasma PGE2 levels correlate with T2DM status and may serve as a marker.
evaluation: Claims C1-C6 are background claims supported by multiple citations to prior literature. These establish the context and motivation for the current study.

result: The mechanism of PGE2 inhibition of GSIS is not fully understood, the impact on nondiabetic β-cell function remains unclear, and the roles of EP1, EP2, and EP4 receptors are rarely reported.
evaluation: Claims C7, C22, and C23 are statements about gaps in current knowledge that motivate the present study. These are supported by the literature review and establish the rationale for the investigation.

result: PGE2 functions through four G protein-coupled receptor subtypes (EP1-4) with distinct signaling properties. EP1 couples to Gq, EP2/EP4 couple to Gs, and EP3 couples to Gi. All four receptors are expressed in pancreatic islets.
evaluation: Claims C8-C12 are background information about EP receptor biology supported by citations to established literature. These provide essential context for understanding the experimental approach.

result: EP3 receptor is highly expressed in diabetic β-cells and is considered the primary effector for PGE2 in GSIS under diabetic conditions. However, evidence suggests EP3 plays a role primarily in T2DM, with limited effects in nondiabetic conditions.
evaluation: Claims C13-C21 are background claims about EP3 receptor function supported by multiple citations. These establish the current understanding that EP3 is important in diabetes but may not be the primary mediator in normal β-cells.

result: Pancreatic β-cells are electrically excitable, GSIS is associated with complex electrical activity regulated by voltage-gated ion channels, and the Kv2 channel family (Kv2.1 and Kv2.2) plays a crucial role in modulating excitability.
evaluation: Claims C24-C27 are background information about β-cell physiology and Kv2 channels supported by citations. These provide essential context for understanding the role of Kv2.2 in insulin secretion.

result: Kv2.1 is the primary facilitator of delayed rectifier K+ currents in rodent β-cells, and suppressing Kv2.1 enhances GSIS in mouse β-cells. However, Kv2.1 inhibitor has little effect on human β-cells, and evidence suggests Kv2.1 regulates insulin secretion through channel clusters independently of electrical function.
evaluation: Claims C28-C32 are background information about Kv2.1 function supported by citations. These establish the context for investigating Kv2.2, which may have different roles than Kv2.1.

result: Human β-cells express both Kv2.1 and Kv2.2 with higher Kv2.2 mRNA levels, Kv2.2 is involved in GSIS, but its in vivo physiological functions have not been definitively established.
evaluation: Claims C33-C35 are background information supported by citations that establish the rationale for investigating Kv2.2 function. The gap in knowledge about Kv2.2 in vivo function motivates the current study.

result: Kv2.2 channels contribute to delayed rectifier outward K+ currents in pancreatic β-cells.
evaluation: Claim C59 is background information supported by citation to Fu et al., 2017. This provides context for the experimental investigation of Kv2.2 in the current study.

result: EP3 may manifest primarily when β-cell dysfunction is established in T2DM, while PGE2 likely exerts its effects via EP2/4 receptors in normal β-cells. In diabetic conditions, PGE2 may act through upregulated EP3 receptors.
evaluation: Claims C93, C98, and C99 are interpretations of the current findings in the context of prior literature. The distinction between normal and diabetic conditions is supported by the experimental data and cited literature, though the diabetic condition was not directly tested in this study.

result: No alterations in β-cell membrane potential were observed following PGE2 treatment, and PGE2 inhibits Kv2.2 channels and β-cell electroactivity via Gs-coupled EP2/4 receptors instead of EP3 receptors.
evaluation: Claims C96-C97 are supported by the experimental data showing no change in membrane potential and the pharmacological evidence for EP2/EP4 involvement. This finding is surprising given expectations based on EP3-Gi signaling.

result: Both Kv2.1 and Kv2.2 contribute to delayed K+ current in human β-cells with lower expression in diabetic islets. Kv2.1 channels exist in clustered and non-clustered forms, with clustered channels being barely conductive. Kv2.1-mediated insulin exocytosis requires clustering and syntaxin 1A interaction but not electrical function.
evaluation: Claims C100-C105 are background information about Kv2.1 and Kv2.2 in human β-cells supported by citations. These provide context for understanding the distinct roles of Kv2.1 (clustering-dependent exocytosis) versus Kv2.2 (electrical function).

result: Kv2.2 channels maintain repetitive action potential firing by promoting recovery of voltage-gated sodium channels from inactivation. Inhibition of Kv2.2 reduces repetitive firing in neurons. The major effect of PGE2-induced Kv2.2 inhibition is to reduce firing rate in β-cells, suggesting Kv2.2 plays a key role in β-cell repetitive firing.
evaluation: Claims C106-C109 integrate prior knowledge about Kv2.2 in neurons (supported by citations) with the current findings in β-cells. The interpretation that Kv2.2 regulates repetitive firing is well-supported by the experimental data showing reduced firing frequency.

result: PGE2-induced reduction in β-cell repetitive firing would decrease calcium channel opening and thus insulin secretion.
evaluation: Claim C110 is a mechanistic inference based on established knowledge about the relationship between action potential firing, calcium influx, and insulin secretion. While not directly tested, this is a well-established principle in β-cell physiology.

result: Kcnb2 knockout mice have similar body weight to wild-type littermates.
evaluation: Claim C111 is supported by experimental data (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C). This control measurement indicates that the knockout does not cause gross metabolic abnormalities.

result: Activation of Gi/o protein-coupled receptors stimulates Na+/K+ ATPase, which hyperpolarizes β-cell membrane potential and suppresses electrical excitability and insulin secretion.
evaluation: Claims C112-C113 are background information about Gi/o signaling supported by citation to Dickerson et al., 2022. This provides context for the expected mechanism of EP3 action, which was not observed in the current study.
